title: Trent Horn vs Matt Dillahunty: Is Belief in the Resurrection Reasonable?
label: Resurrection reasonability and testimony
motion: Is it reasonable to believe Jesus of Nazareth rose from the dead, given historical testimony, expected evidence, background knowledge, and standards for unusual claims?
sourceNote: Assessment based exclusively on the complete locally cached YouTube caption transcript and timestamped events (transcript SHA-256 64097b702db32ced23363716ed92613138cb064628a0da0b8fa25b0b082265f3). Required below-high-confidence audio checks were completed before adjudication; representative quotations must be exact strings from quote-eligible locked source spans.
scoringNote: Scores are AI-generated estimates of argumentative performance under the locked adjudicated-consensus workflow. Repository code calculated every move, section, and overall result once, only after two isolated judgments, required audio review, and disputed-field adjudication closed.
summary: Horn defended resurrection belief through testimony and comparative explanation; Dillahunty narrowly prevailed by separating sincerity from accuracy and emphasizing ordinary error.

pro.text: Reasonable is a lower bar than convincing.
pro.context: Horn used this distinction to argue that responsible evaluators may reasonably accept competing historical explanations without either explanation compelling universal agreement.

con.text: Nobody has to lie for any of this.
con.context: Dillahunty emphasized that sincere mistake or inaccurate transmission can explain resurrection reports without requiring deliberate deception by the witnesses or authors.

pro.words: An unusual-event belief is reasonable when it contradicts no established subject-specific fact, lacks no evidence that should exist if true, and has no equally adequate ordinary explanation.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The enumerated framework is unusually clear, motion-directed, and operational, connecting factual consistency, evidential expectations, and comparative explanation within one intelligible standard for evaluating extraordinary historical beliefs. Principal limitation: The presentation illustrates each requirement more successfully than it establishes their collective sufficiency, leaving unclear why satisfying these three conditions exhausts every relevant dimension of epistemic reasonableness. Live burden: The framework must specify how expected evidence and explanatory equality are measured when surviving historical materials are dependent, incomplete, contested, and interpreted against radically different background probabilities. Locked score: The supplied very-strong band is justified by exceptional relevance, recoverability, and structural coherence, while appropriately retaining space for the underdeveloped sufficiency bridge and evidential measurement problem.

con.words: A claim is reasonable when it remains consistent with what disciplined inquiry establishes as true and possible within reality, regardless of whether the claim ultimately proves true.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The response offers a concise competing standard grounded in shared inquiry, background knowledge, and bias-reducing methods, thereby contacting the affirmative's foundational account of reasonable unusual-event belief. Principal limitation: What qualifies as known possibility or consistency with reality remains underspecified, potentially making unfamiliar event types inadmissible before sufficiently strong evidence can revise the relevant background understanding. Live burden: The negative must explain how its criterion permits evidence-driven expansion of recognized possibilities while still assigning appropriately demanding evidential requirements to claims conflicting with extremely stable experience. Locked score: The supplied strong-and-competent band fits the move's high relevance, clear alternative criterion, and calibrated acknowledgment of residual subjectivity, while preserving reservations about definitional incompleteness and only partial comparison with the affirmative's three conditions.

pro.words: Reasonableness is less demanding than personal conviction, so well-informed evaluators may reasonably endorse competing historical explanations even though neither explanation persuades everyone considering the same evidence.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The reply directly distinguishes reasonable acceptance from personal conviction and explains why historically underdetermined questions can permit informed disagreement without reducing reasonableness to universal persuasiveness. Principal limitation: Different conviction thresholds do not themselves make each competing view adequately warranted, and the response somewhat compresses the negative's objective appeal to background knowledge into personal dissatisfaction. Live burden: The affirmative must demonstrate that resurrection independently clears an appropriate evidential threshold, not merely that reasonable disagreement exists or that some evaluators remain unconvinced. Locked score: The supplied very-strong band reflects outstanding motion relevance, precise threshold distinctions, comprehensive responsiveness, and coherent engagement with both opposing moves, while retaining reservations about the underdefended adequacy condition and partially weakened representation of the negative standard.

con.words: The negative burden is to defeat the reasonableness of accepting resurrection, not to prove that resurrection never occurred or that contrary belief is independently reasonable.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The response draws an exceptionally precise distinction among proving nonoccurrence, defending reasonable disbelief, and showing that affirmative acceptance lacks adequate warrant, thereby clarifying the actual debate burden. Principal limitation: The burden clarification does not itself establish the evidential threshold or demonstrate that the affirmative case falls beneath it, so its success remains procedural rather than substantively dispositive. Live burden: The negative must apply this accurate burden framing to the historical materials and ordinary alternatives, showing why warranted withholding follows without quietly converting nonacceptance into evidence of nonoccurrence. Locked score: The supplied very-strong band is supported by outstanding coherence, direct motion contact, explicit qualification, and nearly complete responsiveness, while appropriately recognizing that even an excellent burden reframe requires separate evidential execution.

pro.words: Historical testimony constitutes evidence rather than unsupported assertion, while early Christian sources and rapid community formation support authentic experiences behind the disciples' resurrection proclamations.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The argument correctly treats testimony as evidentially admissible and connects early proclamation, community formation, and reported experience into a historically recognizable foundation rather than dismissing ancient evidence categorically. Principal limitation: Its broad reliability language and appeal to universal scholarly agreement compress important distinctions among source proximity, literary dependence, sincere experience, accurate interpretation, and the specific content allegedly experienced. Live burden: The affirmative must demonstrate that the accessible materials reliably support sufficiently independent postmortem experiences and not merely an early, sincere, rapidly transmitted conviction whose underlying cause remains uncertain. Locked score: The supplied strong-and-competent band reflects substantial historical relevance and a coherent testimonial foundation, moderated by underdocumented scholarly generalization, partially unstable scope, and an incompletely defended transmission bridge.

con.words: Because resurrection sources cannot now be questioned, confidently identified, reliably reconciled, or physically corroborated, even purported eyewitness material cannot by itself establish the resurrection conclusion.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The move identifies concrete source limitations—authorship, accessibility, reconciliation, and corroboration—and connects them directly to both testimonial reliability and the continued availability of transmission-based alternatives. Principal limitation: Its categorical language about irreconcilability and inability to establish the conclusion is broader than the presented examples support, while inaccessible witnesses do not automatically defeat responsible historical inference. Live burden: The negative must demonstrate representative discrepancies, evaluate source independence and provenance, and explain why ordinary critical methods cannot yield enough cumulative warrant for this particular conclusion. Locked score: The supplied strong-and-competent band accurately reflects high responsiveness, clear central relevance, and multiple pertinent reliability challenges, tempered by missing examples, overstated reconciliation claims, and insufficient acknowledgment of legitimate inference from inaccessible ancient evidence.

con.words: Without prior warrant for divine preservation, biblical resurrection narratives must be evaluated as fallible, potentially biased historical sources rather than treated as necessarily accurate or providentially certified.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The argument clearly identifies the circularity involved in treating scripture as necessarily accurate because a preserving deity is already assumed, while preserving the possibility of ordinary source evaluation. Principal limitation: The affirmative's historical case did not depend explicitly on inerrancy, so the autobiographical contrast only partially contacts the ordinary evidential arguments involving early communities, proclamation, and scholarly assessment. Live burden: The negative must evaluate those arguments through specific historical criteria rather than treating rejection of divine certification as sufficient to defeat testimonial weight. Locked score: The supplied strong-and-competent band credits a coherent anti-circularity distinction, stable conditional framing, and relevant caution about bias, while reflecting partial responsiveness, limited source-specific demonstration, and material underrepresentation of the affirmative's actual historical methodology.

pro.words: Legend, deception, and hallucination allegedly explain reported group appearances, conversions, empty-tomb evidence, and sincere proclamation less adequately than the hypothesis that Jesus was resurrected.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The move accepts the proper comparative task and identifies several concrete explanatory targets, including group appearances, unexpected conversions, early proclamation, sincerity, and the reported empty tomb. Principal limitation: It treats multiple contested report features as jointly established while insufficiently separating source dependence, later development, misidentification, interpretive error, and combinations of ordinary mechanisms that need not preserve every detail. Live burden: The affirmative must defend the reliability and independence of each explanandum before showing that a resurrection hypothesis explains the resulting evidence better than appropriately mixed naturalistic alternatives. Locked score: The supplied strong-and-competent band recognizes direct contact with the central comparative bridge and a coherent explanatory structure, while registering materially overstated premises, limited rival analysis, and comparatively weak evidential documentation.

con.words: Mistake, deception, interpretive error, or inaccurate transmission remains more probable than resurrection when supernatural resurrection has not independently been shown possible or probable.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The argument squarely addresses comparative probability, identifies several ordinary mechanisms that require no deliberate dishonesty, and emphasizes that alternative explanations can combine rather than operate in isolation. Principal limitation: It moves too quickly from lacking independent demonstration of resurrection to preferring ordinary error, without quantitatively or qualitatively comparing how well each alternative explains the affirmative's disputed evidence. Live burden: The negative must show that plausible mixtures of mistake, interpretation, and transmission fit the independently warranted historical facts better than resurrection, rather than relying principally on unfamiliarity. Locked score: The supplied very-strong band reflects precise conditional framing, strong central relevance, and charitable recognition of sincere error, while appropriately reserving credit because the prior-probability premise and feature-by-feature comparison remain incomplete.

pro.words: Postmortem Elvis reports differ because identified remains, medical testimony, photographs, impersonators, and familiar faked-death or misidentification explanations provide specific defeaters absent from the resurrection comparison.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The reply diagnoses precise disanalogies rather than merely rejecting the parody, identifying physical remains, medical testimony, photographic evidence, impersonation, and familiar explanations that materially change the evidential comparison. Principal limitation: Defeating equivalence with Elvis sightings does not positively establish the resurrection case, and the argument still depends on whether parallel contrary evidence concerning Jesus should reasonably be expected. Live burden: The affirmative must use the successful diagnostic distinction only proportionately, then return to demonstrating that its own sources and explanatory comparison possess adequate independent warrant. Locked score: The supplied very-strong band reflects exceptional responsiveness, stable terminology, strong evidential specificity, and charitable reconstruction of the analogy, while preserving the important limitation that refuting a parody removes one objection without proving resurrection.

con.words: Even unanimous sincere reports would directly establish widespread belief, not resurrection, because shared interpretive or transmission error can persist despite honesty, confidence, and numerical agreement.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The reply precisely separates experience, sincere description, causal interpretation, and event truth, showing that even widespread agreement does not automatically bridge those epistemically distinct stages. Principal limitation: Its personal analogy demonstrates the possibility of sincere misinterpretation more readily than the comparative probability of a coordinated error across genuinely independent, well-positioned historical witnesses. Live burden: The negative must determine whether the relevant sources are independent and firsthand, then show that shared interpretation or transmission explains their common content better than resurrection. Locked score: The supplied very-strong band is warranted by exceptional coherence, responsiveness, charity, and direct contact with three affirmative moves, while appropriately leaving the empirical independence question and full comparative likelihood assessment unresolved.

sections.title: Background Knowledge, Natural Regularity, and Divine Agency

pro.words: Because changing realities require actualization, an ultimate unactualized cause is proposed whose inferred characteristics include immateriality, timelessness, power, knowledge, necessity, goodness, and personhood.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The argument supplies an independent metaphysical route toward divine possibility, progressing intelligibly from change and actualization to an ultimate cause characterized initially as changeless, immaterial, and timeless. Principal limitation: The transitions from pure actuality to knowledge, goodness, personality, and resurrection-capable agency are substantially compressed, so the full theological conclusion outruns what the selected reasoning directly establishes. Live burden: The affirmative must defend the causal principle, exclude relevant alternatives, derive the additional divine attributes individually, and connect that cause specifically to intentional intervention in first-century history. Locked score: The supplied mixed band appropriately credits relevance, recoverable structure, and serious metaphysical engagement while reflecting materially overstated necessity, partially unstable terminology, missing qualifications, and insufficient warrant for the argument's most consequential attribute transitions.

con.words: Resurrection belief appears reasonable only after accepting unsupported supernatural premises, because ancient writings and the absence of an immediately preferable explanation do not establish supernatural interaction with reality.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The argument exposes a genuine circularity risk: resurrection cannot become the best explanation merely because supernatural agency was assumed available before the historical evidence received independent evaluation. Principal limitation: The claim that reasonable resurrection belief generally requires antecedent supernatural commitment is too broad, since a cumulative historical argument could theoretically supply evidence for an unfamiliar cause. Live burden: The negative must distinguish illegitimate prior assumption from legitimate posterior inference and explain what independent evidence would make supernatural agency an admissible competitor without presupposing the disputed conclusion. Locked score: The supplied strong-and-competent band credits coherent central burden contact, a clearly recoverable circularity concern, and acknowledgment of evidential uncertainty, while reflecting limited support for the generalized psychological claim and incomplete engagement with cumulative inference.

pro.words: Natural regularity makes exceptions identifiable rather than impossible, and sufficiently sincere, reliable testimony can rationally revise previously uniform experience when an apparent exception occurs.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The reply correctly distinguishes strong prior regularity from logical impossibility and explains how testimonial evidence can sometimes expand background knowledge by revealing a previously unknown exception. Principal limitation: The black-swan analogy compares discovery of an ordinary biological instance with reversal of death through supernatural agency, leaving their prior probabilities and testimonial requirements dramatically underexamined. Live burden: The affirmative must identify reliability conditions strong enough to overcome ordinary error and show that resurrection testimony satisfies them, rather than merely proving that experience can sometimes be revised. Locked score: The supplied strong-and-competent band reflects direct engagement, coherent possibility reasoning, and valuable resistance to categorical exclusion, balanced against the analogy's limited parity, partially unstable scope, and incomplete warrant for the specific resurrection inference.

con.words: Inquiry cannot responsibly invoke a nonmaterial domain until that domain is demonstrated and investigators are given a systematic method for examining its alleged interaction with material reality.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The response establishes a clear methodological requirement that supernatural agency must possess independent evidential availability before it can function as an explanatory category in historical investigation. Principal limitation: Requiring systematic scientific investigability may exceed what is necessary for every historical or metaphysical explanation, and the move does not directly answer testimony-based inference to a singular exception. Live burden: The negative must explain why metaphysical reasoning and historical effects cannot jointly warrant nonmaterial agency unless a repeatable investigative method already exists. Locked score: The supplied strong-and-competent band recognizes coherent central relevance, explicit conditions, and disciplined resistance to explanatory labeling, while accounting for partial responsiveness, an arguably excessive scientific-access requirement, and incomplete engagement with the affirmative's testimonial pathway.

pro.words: Resurrection belief is falsifiable in principle because authenticated remains attributable to Jesus or an early apostolic recantation could substantially undermine the historical evidential case.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The response supplies concrete potential defeaters and therefore answers the categorical allegation that no conceivable historical discovery could count meaningfully against the resurrection belief. Principal limitation: The discussion leaves authentication standards and evidential thresholds uncertain, while acknowledging that ambiguous remains would generate curiosity without necessarily falsifying the larger network of claims. Live burden: The affirmative must specify what evidence would decisively lower confidence, how such evidence could be authenticated, and how residual testimonial claims would be reconsidered after a contrary discovery. Locked score: The supplied strong-and-competent band credits conceptual falsifiability, cautious qualification, and relevant subsidiary burden contact, while reflecting partial responsiveness, limited present corroboration, and instability between curiosity, serious undermining, and outright falsification.

con.words: If resurrection were an established phenomenon, confirmed instances should generate scientific publications, major professional recognition, extensive news coverage, and publicly inspectable demonstrations rather than obscure reports.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The reply makes an intuitive expected-evidence prediction, explaining why repeated, confirmed resurrections would produce conspicuous institutional attention, documentation, professional recognition, and publicly inspectable cases. Principal limitation: It shifts between expectations for repeatable contemporary phenomena and the evidential profile of one allegedly unique ancient event, so the publicity prediction does not directly resolve the historical motion. Live burden: The negative must specify which public evidence should remain available if this singular resurrection occurred and why the absence of that evidence is meaningfully more probable under nonoccurrence. Locked score: The supplied mixed band appropriately recognizes a relevant and understandable expected-evidence consideration while reflecting partial responsiveness, unstable scope, limited contact with the divine-possibility argument, and an analogy whose strongest implications concern modern repetition.

pro.words: The assertion that God should have arranged modern documentation needs independent support, while the surviving historical materials might still make resurrection belief reasonable without technologically contemporary evidence.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The response correctly demands justification for a specific divine-disclosure expectation and observes that absence of modern documentation does not automatically invalidate every historically grounded belief. Principal limitation: Asking whether God might possess good reasons supplies no positive account of those reasons and understates the relational rationale supporting the opponent's expectation of accessible evidence. Live burden: The affirmative must articulate plausible divine aims and constraints that predict this disclosure pattern while showing that existing historical evidence remains sufficient under its own expected-evidence condition. Locked score: The supplied strong-and-competent band recognizes direct responsiveness, a proportionate possibility claim, and a legitimate burden challenge, while reflecting speculative counterpossibilities, incomplete positive explanation, and insufficient charity toward the strongest relationship-based argument.

con.words: A deity desiring universal knowledge and loving relationship could provide evidence sufficient for informed belief, so persistent evidential insufficiency counts against the asserted disclosure arrangement.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The reply supplies the previously missing relational rationale for expecting stronger evidence and corrects the suggestion that the negative demands limitless proof or refuses every possible disclosure. Principal limitation: It moves from divine capability and relational desire to universally sufficient provision without examining competing divine aims, noncoercive relationship, human diversity, or what evidential level the prediction entails. Live burden: The negative must defend a detailed expectation showing why a relational deity would probably provide more accessible evidence and why current ambiguity is surprising under that hypothesis. Locked score: The supplied strong-and-competent band reflects direct contact, clear subsidiary relevance, and a meaningful correction of caricature, balanced against materially overstated certainty, limited independent warrant, and insufficient specification of predicted evidence.

pro.words: Multiple sincere witnesses accepting costly punishment can increase testimonial credibility, while rejecting testimony categorically would undermine much otherwise justified knowledge concerning the ancient world.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The move properly limits costly commitment to increasing credibility and accurately observes that testimony is indispensable to most knowledge of ancient history, preventing an indiscriminate dismissal of testimonial evidence. Principal limitation: It overstates the negative position as abandoning ancient history and does not establish witness independence, direct access, accurate interpretation, or why costly sincerity favors resurrection over sincere mistake. Live burden: The affirmative must separate ordinary historical reliance from warrant for a singular extraordinary conclusion and demonstrate that the relevant commitments reliably trace to firsthand evidential access. Locked score: The supplied mixed band credits relevant defense of testimonial method and a qualified sincerity inference, while reflecting partial responsiveness, representational overreach, weak source-independence support, and failure to answer the strongest ordinary-error alternative.

con.words: Temporally remote hearsay without physical corroboration is insufficient for accepting an unverifiable resurrection claim carrying life-defining religious consequences, especially when witnesses cannot be examined.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The reply directly links testimonial inaccessibility, absent physical corroboration, temporal remoteness, and religious significance to the motion-level question of whether accepting resurrection is epistemically warranted. Principal limitation: Courtroom admissibility, historical justification, physical evidence, verifiability, and falsifiability are treated too interchangeably, making the proposed evidential threshold stronger and less discriminating than the argument independently establishes. Live burden: The negative must formulate a historically appropriate sufficiency standard that acknowledges justified testimonial knowledge while explaining why these particular sources cannot meet the heightened requirement for resurrection. Locked score: The supplied strong-and-competent band recognizes excellent responsiveness and decisive burden contact, while accounting for terminological instability, an underdefended courtroom analogy, and insufficient charity toward evidence-based ancient historical inference.

pro.words: Costly apostolic commitment supports sincerity rather than truth directly, yet sincere resurrection belief still demands explanation, and resurrection is proposed as the best available account.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The reply accepts the opponent's decisive sincerity-versus-truth distinction and productively reframes costly commitment as establishing an explanatory datum rather than directly proving resurrection. Principal limitation: It then labels resurrection the best explanation without renewing the comparison against sincere misinterpretation, grief experience, social reinforcement, source dependence, or transmission development. Live burden: The affirmative must show why the disciples' relevant beliefs were independently established, costly, and causally connected to firsthand experiences that ordinary mechanisms explain less adequately. Locked score: The supplied strong-and-competent band reflects excellent charity, coherent reframing, explicit qualification, and strong responsiveness, tempered by dependence on earlier compressed arguments and failure to contact the strongest ordinary-error component within this exchange.

con.words: Willingness to suffer or die may demonstrate sincere commitment, but comparable sacrifices for incompatible religions show that commitment alone cannot establish the underlying proposition's truth.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The reply sharply distinguishes sincerity from accuracy and supports that distinction with incompatible examples of costly religious commitment, directly defeating any inference from martyrdom alone to truth. Principal limitation: Costly commitment was presented as probabilistic evidence rather than deductive proof, so the response must preserve whatever limited evidential contribution sincerity may provide when firsthand access is independently established. Live burden: The negative must explain how much, if any, costly sincerity contributes after controlling for witness access, independence, interpretive error, and transmission uncertainty. Locked score: The supplied very-strong band follows from exceptional coherence, responsiveness, calibration, and representational charity, with the remaining qualification being that successfully restricting martyrdom's evidential role does not independently resolve the broader historical comparison.

strengths: Horn supplied a clear three-part standard linking factual consistency, expected evidence, and comparative explanation directly to the motion's reasonableness threshold.
He correctly defended testimony as an indispensable historical evidence category and resisted treating natural regularity as proof that exceptions are impossible.
His Elvis response identified concrete disanalogies, while his later burden distinction between reasonableness and personal conviction directly addressed the debate's governing threshold.
He accepted that costly commitment establishes sincerity rather than truth directly, then reformulated sincerity as an explanatory datum requiring further analysis.

blunders.text: The comparative resurrection case treated contested group appearances, source independence, rapid verification, and empty-tomb claims as jointly secure without sufficiently defending each premise.
The metaphysical argument moved too quickly from pure actuality to a personal, knowledgeable, good agent capable of intentionally producing this historical resurrection.
The costly-testimony reply exaggerated the negative position as threatening ancient history generally and left sincere error, witness independence, and firsthand access insufficiently answered.

strengths: Dillahunty clearly distinguished defeating reasonable acceptance from proving nonoccurrence, keeping the negative burden accurately aligned with the motion.
He repeatedly separated sincerity, experience, interpretation, and truth, especially in the martyrdom and final consensus replies, preserving ordinary error without alleging dishonesty.
His source critique identified concrete limitations involving authorship, witness accessibility, reconciliation, corroboration, and the possibility of distorted transmission.
He required supernatural agency to receive independent warrant before functioning as an explanation and connected background regularity to comparative probability rather than strict impossibility.

blunders.text: The courtroom analogy and emphasis on physical corroboration imposed requirements that were not sufficiently distinguished from ordinary standards of historical justification.
The publicity argument shifted from repeatable modern resurrections to a unique ancient event, weakening its direct relevance to the surviving historical evidence.
The relational-disclosure argument asserted a strong expectation of universally sufficient evidence without developing a detailed account of divine aims, constraints, or predicted disclosure.

finalArgument.thesis: The AI steelman is that resurrection belief can be reasonable, without being compulsory, if a carefully delimited cumulative historical case raises divine resurrection above serious competing explanations.
premises: Reasonable belief requires neither certainty nor universal persuasion, but it does require evidence that independently clears a publicly defensible threshold.
Early and sincere resurrection proclamation has evidential value only to the extent that provenance, independence, and experiential content can be historically supported.
Costly commitment primarily supports sincerity; its additional value depends upon establishing that witnesses possessed firsthand access and remained independent.
Ordinary alternatives may be combined, but their adequacy must be tested against only those historical facts established independently of the resurrection narratives' theological conclusions.
A metaphysical case for divine agency can adjust explanatory availability only if it establishes relevant agency and interaction, not merely an abstract first cause.
finalArgument.conclusion: Accordingly, accepting resurrection may be reasonable for an evaluator who finds the restricted historical facts, source analysis, and independent divine-agency case cumulatively stronger than the remaining alternatives.

newArguments.title: Discriminating Evidence Matrix
newArguments.text: Instead of asking whether one ordinary theory explains every narrative detail, construct a matrix containing only independently supported facts and score each hypothesis for explanatory scope, auxiliary assumptions, source dependence, and expected counterevidence. Resurrection need not dominate every cell to remain reasonable, but it must outperform mixed ordinary accounts on enough well-supported facts to compensate for its lower prior probability. This method makes the comparison transparent and prevents disputed narrative details from silently determining the result.

newArguments.title: Asymmetric Defeater Commitment
newArguments.text: A responsible affirmative case should announce beforehand what discoveries would materially reduce confidence: strong evidence of literary dependence behind alleged independent appearances, authenticated early recantation, identifiable remains, or evidence that key traditions developed substantially later. Publicly accepting such defeaters gives the historical claim meaningful vulnerability while avoiding the implausible demand that a single ambiguous artifact instantly settle every connected proposition. The resulting position is testable through proportional revision even when definitive experimental repetition is unavailable.

finalArgument.thesis: The AI steelman is that withholding resurrection belief is reasonable because the available evidence does not overcome source uncertainty, ordinary error mechanisms, and the unusually demanding explanatory leap to divine action.
premises: The negative need not establish nonoccurrence; it must show that affirmative acceptance lacks enough warrant after relevant alternatives and uncertainties are included.
Historical testimony can justify beliefs, but evidential weight decreases when authorship, independence, witness access, transmission, and reconciliation remain uncertain.
Sincerity and sacrifice support commitment, yet accuracy additionally requires reliable access, causal interpretation, and protection against shared social or transmission error.
Mixed ordinary mechanisms remain available because different report features may arise through different combinations of experience, interpretation, memory, authorship, and transmission.
Invoking divine action requires evidence for relevant agency and interaction beyond identifying an unexplained event or proposing an abstract metaphysical cause.
finalArgument.conclusion: Therefore, withholding acceptance is proportionate unless source reliability, comparative explanatory advantage, and relevant divine agency are established strongly enough to overcome the accumulated uncertainty.

newArguments.title: Correlated Testimony Discount
newArguments.text: Multiple reports should increase confidence according to their independence, not merely their number. If later accounts share traditions, communities, theological expectations, or literary sources, apparent multiplication may represent correlated transmission rather than separate confirmation. A structured dependence discount would assign less cumulative weight when reports plausibly inherit the same interpretive framework. This does not render the testimony worthless; it prevents numerical accumulation from overstating how much genuinely independent evidence supports the resurrection inference.

newArguments.title: Prediction Without Courtroom Analogy
newArguments.text: The negative can avoid importing courtroom standards by comparing expected evidence under rival hypotheses. If a relational deity intended a resurrection to ground broadly accessible belief, clearer provenance, independent contemporary attestation, durable corroboration, or repeated accessible disclosure would be more expected than the record described here. Ordinary tradition development predicts ambiguity and dependence more readily. This remains a probabilistic argument: competing divine purposes could weaken the prediction, but they require independent specification rather than serving as unrestricted explanations for any evidential pattern.
